patient.chief_complaint: Left eyelid drooping and double vision worsening over 3 months, with arm fatigue and swallowing difficulty
patient.history_present_illness:
A 60-year-old Black Brazilian woman, a primary school teacher, presented to the neurology inpatient unit for evaluation of progressive left eyelid drooping and double vision over three months. She first noticed intermittent left eyelid drooping approximately three months ago, initially occurring only in the late afternoon and early evening after a full teaching day. She and her family attributed the symptoms to work-related fatigue and stress, and she was evaluated by her primary care physician who reassured her that the ptosis was likely related to exhaustion and offered no further investigation.

Over the next six weeks, the ptosis became more persistent and began appearing in the morning as well, though consistently worse by afternoon. She developed horizontal diplopia on leftward gaze approximately six weeks before admission, finding herself tilting her head to compensate. Over the four weeks prior to admission she noticed progressive difficulty swallowing solid foods — bread and rice required additional sips of water. Her voice became nasal and harder to project in large classrooms after sustained speaking. She reported bilateral arm fatigue when lifting classroom objects or washing her hair above her head.

She denied headache, sensory symptoms, neck pain, visual blurring beyond the diplopia, or shortness of breath at rest. She noted no limb weakness at rest. She had seen an ophthalmologist two months earlier who excluded structural lid or orbital pathology and dry eye. There was no antecedent infection, vaccination, or new medication. Symptoms showed a clear diurnal pattern — uniformly better in the morning and after a short midday rest, substantially worse by evening.

CT CHEST WITH CONTRAST

INDICATION: Evaluation of anterior mediastinum; screen for thymoma in patient with suspected neuromuscular junction disorder.

TECHNIQUE: Multidetector CT of the chest with intravenous contrast, axial reconstructions with coronal and sagittal reformats.

COMPARISON: None available.

FINDINGS:
Mediastinum: No anterior mediastinal mass. Thymic tissue not separately visualised; fatty thymic involution consistent with patient age. No mediastinal lymphadenopathy. No hilar adenopathy. Aortopulmonary window unremarkable.
Lungs: No pulmonary nodule, mass, or consolidation. No pleural effusion. No pneumothorax.
Heart and pericardium: Normal cardiac silhouette. No pericardial effusion.
Bones: No lytic or blastic osseous lesion.

IMPRESSION:
1. No anterior mediastinal mass. Age-appropriate fatty thymic involution. No thymoma identified.
2. No mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy.
3. Lungs clear.
Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

INDICATION: Suspected neuromuscular junction disorder; fatigable ptosis and proximal weakness.

TECHNIQUE: Low-rate (3 Hz) repetitive nerve stimulation of the accessory nerve recording trapezius, facial nerve recording nasalis, and radial nerve recording anconeus. Surface electrodes. Temperature maintained ≥32°C. Rest intervals 1 min between trials.

RESULTS:
  Trapezius (accessory nerve, 3 Hz): Baseline CMAP amplitude 6.8 mV; decrement 13% (1st to 4th response) — ABNORMAL (threshold >10%)
  Nasalis (facial nerve, 3 Hz): Baseline CMAP amplitude 1.4 mV; decrement 15% — ABNORMAL
  Anconeus (radial nerve, 3 Hz): Baseline CMAP amplitude 5.2 mV; decrement 11% — ABNORMAL

POST-EXERCISE FACILITATION (10-second maximal voluntary contraction):
  Partial repair of decrement immediately post-exercise; decrement returns toward baseline by 2–3 minutes — post-activation exhaustion pattern.

HIGH-RATE RNS (50 Hz):
  Trapezius: CMAP increment 6% — no pathological facilitation (well below >100% threshold for pre-synaptic pattern).

BASELINE CMAP AMPLITUDES: Normal at all tested sites.

NEEDLE EMG (deltoid, orbicularis oculi, first dorsal interosseous):
  Normal insertional activity. No fibrillation potentials. No positive sharp waves. No fasciculations. Motor unit morphology: normal duration, amplitude, and polyphasia. Normal recruitment.

SENSORY NCS: Normal velocities and amplitudes; no evidence of peripheral neuropathy.

IMPRESSION: Abnormal decremental CMAP responses at 3 Hz at trapezius (13%), nasalis (15%), and anconeus (11%). Post-exercise partial repair followed by exhaustion pattern. No pathological 50-Hz facilitation. Normal baseline CMAP amplitudes and normal needle EMG. Findings are consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission at the postsynaptic junction. Clinical correlation recommended.

specialized_test.impression: Abnormal decremental responses at 3 Hz: trapezius 13%, nasalis 15%, anconeus 11%. Post-exercise exhaustion pattern. No 50-Hz facilitation. Findings consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission

output.interpretation: AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 8.7 nmol/L (reference < 0.4 nmol/L). AChR blocking and modulating antibodies both elevated. Anti-MuSK and anti-LRP4 negative. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with autoimmune neuromuscular junction disorders; an elevated binding antibody is associated with postsynaptic neuromuscular junction dysfunction
abnormal_values_summary: AChR binding antibody 8.7 nmol/L (markedly elevated; reference < 0.4 nmol/L)

findings.description:
ICE PACK TEST

INDICATION: Evaluation of left ptosis.

TECHNIQUE: Crushed ice in a surgical glove applied to the left closed eyelid for 2 minutes. Levator excursion measured immediately before and after application.

RESULTS:
  Pre-application: Left levator excursion 6 mm.
  Post-application (2 minutes): Left levator excursion 10 mm — improvement of 4 mm.

IMPRESSION: Positive ice pack test — ≥2 mm improvement in ptosis following cold application. Findings support a disorder with neuromuscular junction fatigability as substrate for ptosis. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: Positive ice pack test: 4 mm improvement in left levator excursion after 2-minute cold application. Supports a fatigable substrate for ptosis

findings.description:
BEDSIDE RESPIRATORY FUNCTION TESTING

INDICATION: Bulbar and mild proximal limb involvement; respiratory monitoring in suspected neuromuscular junction disorder.

MEASUREMENTS:
  FVC: 2.8 L (predicted 2.6 L; 108% predicted) — within normal limits
  NIF (Negative Inspiratory Force): -62 cmH2O (threshold for concern: < -60 cmH2O) — adequate
  MEP (Maximum Expiratory Pressure): 74 cmH2O (reference ≥ 60 cmH2O) — adequate

IMPRESSION: Respiratory function within normal limits. FVC and NIF values do not indicate immediate respiratory compromise. Serial monitoring is advised given bulbar involvement. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: FVC 2.8 L (108% predicted); NIF -62 cmH2O; MEP 74 cmH2O. No immediate respiratory compromise

results.title: International consensus guidance for management of myasthenia gravis (Sanders 2016)
results.content:
MYASTHENIA GRAVIS — CLASSIFICATION AND MANAGEMENT

MGFA CLASSIFICATION (Jaretzki 2000):
  Class I: Ocular only.
  Class II: Mild generalised. IIa predominantly limb/axial; IIb predominantly bulbar/respiratory.
  Class III: Moderate generalised.
  Class IV: Severe generalised.
  Class V: Intubation required.

DIAGNOSTIC FRAMEWORK:
  AChR antibody positive in ~85% of generalised MG; MuSK positive in ~6% of seronegatives; LRP4 in a further subset.
  RNS >10% decrement at 2-3 Hz supports postsynaptic NMJ disease (sensitivity ~75% in generalised MG).
  Single-fiber EMG: sensitivity >95%, reserved for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases.
  CT chest mandatory in all confirmed cases for thymoma screening.

TREATMENT HIERARCHY:
  Symptomatic: pyridostigmine 30–60 mg every 4–6 hours titrated to effect.
  Immunosuppression: prednisone (gradual dose escalation); steroid-sparing (azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil).
  Rescue: IVIG 2 g/kg over 2–5 days; plasmapheresis (PLEX) for crisis or pre-operative optimisation.
  Thymectomy: indicated for thymoma; also recommended for non-thymoma AChR+ generalised MG (MGTX trial, Wolfe 2016) in patients ≤65 years.

Evidence level: RCT (MGTX trial for thymectomy); multiple RCTs for IVIG/PLEX; observational for steroid-sparing agents.
results.finding: MGFA Class IIa generalised MG: mild generalised weakness predominantly affecting limbs/axial muscles with ocular involvement; management with pyridostigmine plus immunosuppression; thymectomy considered per MGTX criteria.

output.proposed: pyridostigmine initiation in a patient on losartan; screen for MG-exacerbating agents
interactions: PYRIDOSTIGMINE + LOSARTAN: No clinically significant pharmacokinetic interaction. Cholinergic stimulation from pyridostigmine may produce mild bradycardia; at standard doses with losartan (an ARB without cardiac conduction effects) this is not clinically significant. Routine heart rate monitoring appropriate.
AMINOGLYCOSIDES (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin): Block presynaptic and postsynaptic neuromuscular junction; can precipitate myasthenic crisis in MG patients. Contraindicated unless no alternative.
FLUOROQUINOLONES (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin): FDA black-box warning — may exacerbate neuromuscular blockade in patients with myasthenia gravis. Avoid.
TELITHROMYCIN (ketolide antibiotic): Contraindicated in myasthenia gravis — associated with fatal myasthenic exacerbation.

MAGNESIUM (IV): High-dose IV magnesium inhibits acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction; may precipitate crisis in MG. Avoid IV magnesium (including magnesium sulfate for eclampsia prophylaxis or pre-eclampsia management) unless no alternative available.
BETA-BLOCKERS (propranolol, metoprolol, atenolol): May worsen neuromuscular blockade at the junction; use with caution if clinically necessary. Cardioselective agents at low dose carry lower risk.
NEUROMUSCULAR BLOCKERS (vecuronium, pancuronium, rocuronium): Prolonged and unpredictable blockade in MG; use only under anaesthesia with dose reduction and close monitoring.
contraindications: High-dose IV magnesium — avoid in MG unless no alternative
warnings: Fluoroquinolones: avoid; FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers: use only with anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing
Do not initiate high-dose corticosteroids as outpatient monotherapy — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5–10
alternatives: Ambenonium chloride: alternative cholinesterase inhibitor if pyridostigmine not tolerated

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIa)

differential.key_features: TSH and free T4 normal; no proptosis or lid retraction; ophthalmoplegia is fatigable (not restrictive), resolves with cooling — incompatible with thyroid orbitopathy.
Initial attribution to fatigue/stress; however, objective Cogan lid twitch, positive ice-pack test, clear fatigability, and positive AChR serology establish organic disease.
LEMS shows reduced baseline CMAPs with pathological >100% increment at 50-Hz RNS; here baseline CMAPs normal, 50-Hz increment only 6%, and AChR antibody markedly positive.
MuSK-MG is typically bulbar-predominant with poor RNS decrement in limb muscles; anti-MuSK negative here.
No tongue atrophy or fasciculations; no upper motor neuron signs; RNS decrement (not fibrillations or fasciculations) with positive AChR antibody makes ALS untenable.

optimal_actions.action: Order serologies: anti-AChR (binding, blocking, modulating), anti-MuSK, anti-LRP4, and TSH/free-T4 for thyroid autoimmunity
optimal_actions.expected_finding: AChR binding antibody markedly elevated; TSH normal — excludes thyroid orbitopathy as confounder

optimal_actions.action: Order repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) at 3 Hz across proximal and facial muscles
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Decrement >10% in trapezius, nasalis, and anconeus — confirms postsynaptic NMJ disorder

optimal_actions.action: Order CT chest with contrast for thymoma screening
Search literature for MGFA classification and current MG treatment guidance
optimal_actions.expected_finding: MGFA classification; pyridostigmine, immunosuppression, thymectomy evidence base (MGTX trial); IVIG/PLEX for crisis

useless_tools.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Brain MRI is non-contributory in typical generalised MG; reserved for cases where an alternative CNS cause (brainstem lesion, demyelination) is genuinely in the differential.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG in the absence of independent cardiac comorbidity.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.

sequence_constraints.reason: Order AChR/MuSK/LRP4 serologies first; single-fiber EMG is reserved for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases — resource stewardship and diagnostic hierarchy.

critical_actions: Confirm AChR binding antibody positivity — here markedly elevated at 8.7 nmol/L
Perform RNS at 2-3 Hz in proximal and facial muscles to document NMJ decrement
Order CT chest with contrast to screen for thymoma in every confirmed MG patient
Initiate pyridostigmine and plan immunosuppression (prednisone, steroid-sparing agent)
Document baseline FVC and NIF given bulbar symptoms; repeat q4h if clinical deterioration
Screen all new prescriptions against MG-exacerbating drug list
contraindicated_actions: Do NOT prescribe aminoglycoside antibiotics (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin) — risk of precipitating myasthenic crisis
Do NOT prescribe fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) — FDA black-box warning for MG exacerbation
Do NOT prescribe telithromycin — contraindicated in MG; associated with fatal exacerbation
Do NOT administer IV magnesium without alternative — inhibits acetylcholine release at NMJ and may precipitate crisis
Do NOT use non-depolarising neuromuscular blockers without anaesthesia/MG-aware dosing protocols
Do NOT initiate high-dose corticosteroids as sole outpatient therapy without a pyridostigmine bridge — risk of paradoxical worsening at days 5-10
Do NOT attribute fluctuating fatigable ptosis and proximal weakness to functional disorder or stress without completing serology, RNS, and ice-pack test
key_reasoning_points: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with clear diurnal pattern (worse in evening, better after rest) is the hallmark of MG — initial attribution to stress and fatigue is the classic delay and should raise rather than lower MG suspicion when symptoms are objectively progressive.
The ice-pack test (4 mm improvement in levator excursion) provides rapid low-cost bedside corroboration of fatigable ptosis before laboratory results are available.

AChR antibody positivity (~85% sensitivity in generalised MG) combined with unambiguous RNS decrement (>10% at multiple sites) is sufficient for diagnosis in a typical presentation — single-fiber EMG is reserved for seronegative or RNS-non-diagnostic cases.

CT chest for thymoma is mandatory in every confirmed MG case, regardless of clinical picture; here negative (age-appropriate involution), but this does not change the thymectomy consideration based on MGTX trial evidence for non-thymoma AChR+ generalised MG.
The 50-Hz RNS increment of only 6% (well below the >100% threshold) excludes a presynaptic (Lambert-Eaton) pattern, as does the normal baseline CMAP amplitude.

MG-exacerbating drugs — aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers — must be screened against every new prescription; a single dose can precipitate crisis.

red_herrings.data_point: Initial attribution of ptosis and fatigue to work-related stress and exhaustion by primary care physician
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchoring on functional or psychosomatic aetiology, delaying neuromuscular workup.
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Fluctuating, fatigable, diurnal ptosis is a red flag for MG; improvement with rest and worsening with sustained use is the pathognomonic pattern — symptoms attributed to fatigue that are objectively progressive and demonstrably fatigable by examination mandate serological and electrophysiological workup for NMJ disease.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (labs, RNS, CT-chest, literature, drug-interactions), classic unambiguous AChR+ generalized MG with clear decrement and positive antibody; single red herring (initial fatigue/stress attribution); no thymoma; no seronegative complexity — straightforward tier by rubric.

metadata.real_seed: constructed from typical published presentation of AChR-positive generalised MG (MGFA Class IIa) in a middle-aged woman; presentation loosely parallels the epidemiological profile described in Gilhus 2016 (NEJM 375:2570-2581) and Sanders 2016 consensus; no individual PMID verified for a matching case report — PMID not fabricated per real-seeding rule.
metadata.what_makes_it_different: Unique in the MG set: (1) female patient (all existing RS cases are male), (2) Black Brazilian ethnicity (all existing cases are South Asian, White, or unspecified), (3) straightforward difficulty with no thymoma and no anti-titin positivity, (4) red herring is purely historical (initial stress/fatigue attribution) rather than a misleading comorbidity or lab value, (5) ice-pack test explicitly positive as a recommended initial bedside tool.
